title: Rubrik report: 28 per cent of ransomware victims took longer than six weeks to recover
geo_basis: global report; the source gives no location, so the pin is a placeholder
summary: Rubrik's Global Threat Landscape Report 2026, as published by iTWire, analyses nearly 17,000 publicly reported incidents from January to October 2026. It says organisations took a median of 20 days to fully restore, 32 per cent of ransomware victims were back within two weeks, and for 28 per cent it took longer than six weeks. Exploited vulnerabilities were 54 per cent of identified entry points.
plain: A Rubrik study of nearly 17,000 reported attacks says 28 per cent of ransomware victims needed more than six weeks to recover, and exploited software flaws were the most common way in.
exec: Rubrik reports a median of 20 days to fully restore after ransomware, and 28 per cent of victims taking longer than six weeks.
action: General advice: patch internet-facing systems, since Rubrik found exploited vulnerabilities were 54 per cent of identified entry points, and test that backups are protected and restorable.

sources.name: iTWire (guest research, Rubrik): More Than One in Four Organisations Are Still Recovering Six Weeks After a Cyber Attack, Report Finds

date_note: Dated by the iTWire article (23 November AEDT), which says Rubrik released the report that day; Rubrik's own report page answered 403 and was not read.

validation.note: Only iTWire's guest-research article (vendor-supplied text from Rubrik) read; Rubrik's report page and newsroom answered 403.

evidence.quote: analyses nearly 17,000 publicly reported incidents and tracks 100 ransomware groups active between January and October 2026
Organisations took a median of 20 days to fully restore after recovery operations began.
Fewer than one in three ransomware victims (32 per cent) were back up and running within two weeks while for 28 per cent of organisations it took longer than six weeks.
Exploited vulnerabilities were the most common entry point, accounting for 54 per cent of those identified, followed by compromised credentials (18 per cent) and phishing (14 per cent).
